If shifts call for a distinct window, modify your log only with joint confirmation. Avoid always asking Bo to fill in just for Bo's constant working hours. A swap habit always giving Bo additional work calls for a discussion about workloads, not an assumption of bad motivation.

Privacy and own rooms

Focus your rota on communal rooms. An adult must opt in for any job in that adult's own room. Do not go into anybody's own room for photos or to audit stray goods. If a room's condition disrupts communal activity, discuss actual impact and a joint plan.

Goods in a living room can go to a joint holding spot, with a window for pickup. Do not discard goods or put goods in an additional adult's room without confirmation. Your pact might call for pickup by day 2, with common walking paths always allowing normal transit. Actual timings must fit your flat, not this illustration.

Products by joint pact

Raj's wish for products without aroma additions calls for a joint shopping plan. Ask what products fit and what info Raj wants to confirm. A familiar brand cannot justify assuming a product fits; point to an actual product. Raj can ask for a product without supplying a diagnosis.

Pick communal products jointly and fix how costs will split. If a product on your list is not in stock, ask prior to swapping it for a distinct product. An aroma Bo wants cannot justify ignoring Raj's pact with your group. Put products in a spot all four can find, following actual product instructions.

A missing job

Say Mina cannot finish A following a shift modification. Ask away from a public group chat: "Bathroom A still awaits finishing. Could you do it by tomorrow, or should all of us confirm a swap?" Focus on missing work and a practical plan, not an insult.

If Bo fills in, log Bo's work and jointly fix a following allocation. Do not allow a stand-in job to turn into an ongoing addition without discussion. Do not add sanctions that all four did not confirm. Ongoing missing jobs call for a capacity discussion and a plan that can actually work.

Discuss at day 14

Hold a short discussion at day 14. Ask how minimums fit actual jobs, which jobs took additional work, how windows fit shifts and if communal rooms could support normal activity. Allow all four to talk without butting in. Talk from your log, but allow all adults to add an account of what got in a task's way.

Pick 1 or 2 modifications, such as splitting a big allocation or clarifying a bathroom minimum. Put modifications in writing and try a following block. Carry on with what works. A rota can grow from actual trials without starting from scratch.

A fair plan puts work into a common log, honors privacy and allows fluctuating shifts. It grants adults a way to discuss missing work without insults.

prompt: Write a complete original fantasy story about a young cartographer on an island whose paths shift at each dawn. Establish three clear rules for the shifting paths, including one stable feature that can be used for navigation. The cartographer must find a home that appears to have vanished, using observations and the rules rather than a newly invented magical power. Include setbacks, meaningful dialogue, a fair clue and a satisfying resolution. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of natural, substantive English, with no padding.
response:
On our island, a map could go wrong whilst its ink was still drying. I thought drawing maps was a bold occupation. Hari, who paid for my ink, thought a map must say which day it was drawn.

At 18 I had drawn my top map so far: six paths flowing out from Black Pillar, all curls and tidy arcs. Nan's small hut sat at its north rim, with a thin brass rod rising from its roof. I had drawn that rod with a hair. I had not put in fork posts. Such posts spoilt my arcs.

Our island had 3 laws about paths. First, paths shift at dawn and stay still until dawn again. Also, paths can curl and turn, but all joins stay intact and fork posts go with paths. Third, apart from paths and fork posts, all land and buildings stay put. Black Pillar cannot shift; all six main paths still start at that pillar. At all forks, posts with symbols mark branching arms.

No council could modify such laws. As a child, I lost a doll as a path slid away from its snug spot in a ditch. Our dining nook did not shift an inch. All locals grow up knowing this. Putting such facts into a map can still call for much thought.

Hari saw my work by lamplight. "Grand. How can a visitor find your Nan?"

"North from our pillar. Follow that long loop toward our mill."

"Today."

I put my thumb on "Drawn 3 May" at its bottom. Hari said OK, but did not buy a copy. His map was for our mill's cart. A cart must know much apart from how smoothly I could draw an arc.

That night Nan had a boy bring down a card. LUNCH AT MY HUT. BRING MY INK JAR. Down from its words Nan had drawn a fish, a half moon, and a cup with a loop at its flank. I thought such small drawings put a bit of charm into Nan's card. I put it in my tin box, away from damp. I could shut that box firmly. I had bought it for important plans. Now I got back to Nan's brass rod.

At dawn a low scraping sound slid past our door. Our paths found unfamiliar positions. No building shook. Through my window I saw our path curl toward our dock, not toward our mill as it did prior to dawn. Following food, I put Nan's ink in my bag and took my grand map to Black Pillar.

From that spot I could find north without a doubtful assumption. Our dock was south of that pillar, our mill toward sundown, and Nan's hut north. All 3 buildings still sat in familiar spots. Facing north, I found a path turning roughly that way. Its first post had two tiny fish, but I was looking at a path's form, not its marks.

For half an hour I took paths most akin to my map. At a fork I took a curling arm. At a long loop I swung toward our mill again. A path wound round a hill and brought my boots to a dry pit. A cart lay in bits at its bottom. No hut, no brass rod, no Nan.

I stood with my map in both hands. For an instant I had a childish thought that our island had lost Nan and Nan's hut. But I caught that thought. Buildings did not shift. Our laws did not allow it, so I was in a wrong spot. My own assumptions could go wrong; our island's laws could not.

Kit was loading grit into a cart by that pit. "Looking for anything?"

"My Nan's hut."

Kit saw my bag. "Still north. You now stand by our mill."

"That path ran north."

"It did at its start."

Kit did not say it unkindly. His work was matching loads to a cart with a split rim, and my bag was blocking his work. I shut my map. "Which path runs back to Black Pillar?" Kit put up an arm toward that path I had just trod. All joins still stood intact, so going back along it would put my boots at my starting spot. I trod that path backward, looking hard at all its marks now.

At that pillar I took out Nan's card. Fish, half moon, cup. I had drawn how a path might look from a sky full of gulls. Nan had drawn how to follow it on foot. Such small drawings had a job apart from charm. I could almost catch Nan saying, Why would I put ink into a charming fish as I am asking for additional ink?

I took a look round all six starting posts. Two had fish. A post had a pair swimming apart; its companion had a fat fish with a blunt tail. I had trod past that post as its path ran south, back toward our dock. Now I took Nan's first mark as it was: a solitary fish.

I hung back. My grand map put Nan's brass rod at its top. That path with a solitary fish ran away from it. But a path could curl without losing its joins. Its initial compass point could not say how it would finish. I put my map away and took that fish path.

My path ran south for a stint, and swung back round a clump of birch. I could spot Black Pillar among trunks. Going round it did not shift that pillar. I was simply looking from a distinct spot. At our first fork, both arms had moon marks: a full moon and a half moon. I almost took full moon as that arm ran north. Nan had drawn half. I took half.

Rain hit whilst I was making a rough copy of that turn in charcoal. I sought to guard it with my coat, but drops got onto it. My fish was a blot and my moon lost its straight rim. My grand map in my bag still sat dry. It would look odd if my only surviving map was a path to a grit pit.

Nan's card was still in its tin box. I put away my damp copy, took out that original, and sought a cup. I did not hurry simply as my work was damp. I had lost an hour hurrying along a path that fit my drawing.

At our following fork, a cup stood on both posts. A post had a plain bowl on a foot. Its companion had a loop at its flank. Nan's ink put a tiny gap at its loop. That cut symbol had a matching gap. I had thought Nan's cup was awkward. Now that awkward bit could stop a tidy wrong turn.

I took that cup with a loop. Past it, a narrow path ran by a low wall. A branch lay across all room a cart would want. I could walk round it, but Hari's cart could not. I put that branch on a scrap and put "4 May" by it. Our shifting laws had not put a branch in a cart's way. It lay on ordinary ground. A good map ought to say which sort of difficulty it put forward.

That wall ran uphill. My path did not. It swung sharply down and ran up a hollow's far rim. I saw a thin brass rod through birch boughs, right north of Black Pillar, at Nan's old spot. I had drawn its thin ink mark rightly. I had simply not drawn all that a visitor must know to find it.

Nan stood by a door with an apron on an arm. "Your soup is waiting."

"I thought your hut was lost."

"My roof still drips in its usual spot."

I put down Nan's ink. Nan put it away and took a look at my damp charcoal hands. I told Nan about that pit, Kit, and two fish. Nan found joy in that bit about fish, but not in that part that was scary. Nan told how my granddad put a morning into walking toward his brass rod and finally got to a goat hut.

"Did Granddad draw maps?" I said.

"No. Granddad had no way to justify that trip."

At lunch I put my grand map on our board. Nan thought my brass rod was good. I put down my path's marks: fish, half moon, cup with a loop. Down from it I put full moon and plain cup as opposing options, with words saying I did not go down both. I did not claim to know such paths just by spotting initial marks.

"Is this ugly?" I said.

"I could follow it with aid."

That hurt, but it was also good information. Nan could not say if my half moon stood for a fork or a night to walk. I put my symbols on drawings of posts, with arrows from post to post. I put Black Pillar first and Nan's door last. Such symbols could not vanish among my curls now.

Nan put a hand by my branch. "Why is that by a cup?" I told how it could block Hari's cart. Nan said last night's wind put it down, and a local might shift it by dusk. I put down that I saw it this morning, not that it was part of this path for all days. "Would a public map to your door suit you?" I said.

"Only if all visitors bring ink," Nan said, smiling. "No. This copy is for our family."

I put "Nan" on its back, out of public sight. Hari's mill map must hold our mill's marks and cart widths, not Nan's lunch path. My grand map sought to do all jobs without asking who would carry it.

I did not go back that night, partly for Nan's food and partly to try my drawing following dawn. Following dawn, that path out from Nan's door ran uphill. Looking out last night, I saw it run down into a hollow. I trod past cup, half moon, fish, sticking to original joins. Black Pillar stood at my finish. My own boots and Nan's old marks could claim that triumph.

Hari stood by it with his cart. I put both maps in his hands, and told him about that branch. "Is it still blocking a cart?" Hari said. I said it did not block my walk this morning, but I could not say if any cart path still ran past it. Hari had a grin and put a blank scroll in my hands.

"Start with what our cart must know."

I put Black Pillar first. Now I sought our mill's fork marks. In my bag, Nan's small map sat snug in its tin box. At its top I had put a plain tag: Lunch. At its bottom I put 5 May and a blank row for our following walk.

prompt: Write a connected practical guide for four fictional students producing a one-page school bulletin every month with teacher supervision. The page has room for three short articles, an announcement box, and one original drawing. Explain choosing an audience and purpose, gathering accurate information, assigning roles, drafting, editing for clarity, checking names and dates, arranging the page, obtaining the teacher's final review, and distributing the approved page. Include a concrete four-week production schedule, a sample article brief, a compact editing checklist, and a small mock page outline. Cover a late article, two students wanting the same role, an incorrect date caught after distribution, and a student who wants to contribute without being named. Do not invent school policy or give legal advice. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive useful guidance.
response:
A small school journal should do a plain job: allow pupils to find out what was, what is coming, and how to join in. Four pupils can do this on 1 folio if all opt for a small goal and work with a tutor throughout. Final approval should not act as a last-instant shock.

First ask who will look at it. For your class, familiar pupils and rooms might allow a short account. A journal for all pupils may call for additional information. Ask your tutor how a final copy can go out. Do not add a school policy or act as if all pupils can go to a particular chat without asking.

Hold your format in sight: 3 short accounts, a box for what's on, and an original drawing. All must fit 1 folio. An additional account must push a part out, not turn 1 folio into 2 without discussion. Pick parts that aid pupils, not just anything that will fill a gap.

A goal could say: "Our monthly journal shows 3 parts of school days and aids pupils in finding club tasks." This can inform a pick if 2 parts want a spot. A part might fit a following month, though it sounds good now. All four should say what fits; a bold pupil should not hold all authority.

A 4-part monthly plan

Days1-7: pick accounts, list facts to find out, and assign jobs.
Days8-14: find information, draft all 3 accounts, and plan a drawing.
Days15-21: trim, audit who/which day/what hour, and build a full copy.
Days22-28: obtain tutor approval, fix flaws, hand out prints, and log what should shift.

Do not put a final audit at distribution's actual instant. Allow a gap for your tutor to look and for pupils to act on that input. Work backward from your distribution day. Ask how long a tutor wants to do an audit, not how long you wish it would last.

A fictional job split could put Ali on planning accounts, Boris on auditing facts, Mina on art and layout, and Noor on draft tracking and distribution. A job is not a claim to block input. All 4 can draft, put in thoughts, and ask why. Swap jobs following a monthly run so nobody must always act as coordinator.

Hold a joint task log with task, pupil, cutoff, what is going on now, and following action. For illustration: "Club account | Ali | day10 | draft in | Boris to confirm club start hour." A status should say what is blocking a task, not just "working on it."

If 2 pupils want a matching job, ask what is good about it for both. Both could split a job this month, with a plain division, or swap months. Do not award a job automatically to a loud pupil. A pupil not doing a first-pick job should still do important work, not just tidying.

Planning an account

An account plan should say topic, who it is for, main point, facts to find out, a word limit, and who can confirm facts. Do not script all wording. A fictional account about a lunch drawing nook could say how to join, not claim all pupils find it fun.

A fictional plan might say: "Topic: drawing nook. Public: pupils not familiar with it. Goal: how to join. Facts: room, days, start and finish hour, tutor on duty, and what to bring. Limit:70 words. Audit:ask that tutor." Put doubtful points in a list until an actual contact confirms all of it.

Find information from an adult running a club or from actual school handouts. Log who said what and which day you did an audit. A class buddy can point to a fact, but bold claims from an old account cannot supply proof. If accounts clash, go to your tutor with a narrow prompt about that clash.

Hold what you saw, quotation, and opinion apart. If a pupil says a club was fun, say who thought so; do not turn it into a claim that all pupils found it fun. Ask that pupil to audit a quotation. Do not add approval to an account just to jazz it up.

To audit a room clash, log both claims: Ali was told room3, but a handout says room4. Ask that club's tutor which fits and if a prior handout is old. Do not pick room3 just as Ali says it firmly. Put that tutor's solution in your log and modify all parts of your journal that list a room. A fact audit should follow a claim into all its locations.

A compact draft audit

Is a main point obvious from our start?
Do all accounts hold facts pupils want?
Who confirms orthography, days, hours, and locations?
Do quotations match what was said?
Is what's on in a box, with a plain action?
Is art original and part of our topic?
Can all of it fit 1 folio?
Did our tutor say OK to this actual draft?

Apply this list to all of your journal, not only your own account. Look for a main point first, and small facts following that. A smooth paragraph can still hold a faulty day or a fault in a pupil's public tag. Audit orthography, not only how smooth a draft sounds.

If you trim a class buddy's draft, say why it aids your goal. Try: "Room and start hour aid a pupil joining now. Could both go prior to that long account of a club's past?" Ask its author to do a trim if it can fit. Trimming should aid a joint journal, not claim a buddy's job.

A mock layout

Top: journal tag, month, and short goal.
Top A: account1, our main account.
Top B: account2, a distinct part of a school day.
Bottom A: account3, short.
Bottom B: original drawing and short caption.
Foot: box for what's on, with day, hour, location, and action.

This is a mock layout, not an actual school form. Draw it roughly prior to polishing words. If art calls for additional room, cut words thoughtfully, not by making print so small pupils cannot follow it. A trim must hold all important facts. Cut duplication first.

Put obvious captions on accounts and allow gaps so pupils can spot distinct parts. Ask a pupil not in your group to find what's on and say what to do. If that pupil cannot find it, layout still calls for work. Your own familiarity is not proof of a good layout.

If an account is past its cutoff, ask what is missing and fix a practical final cutoff within your group. Supply a narrow kind of aid: confirm a fact or trim a long draft. Do not hand a full account to a pupil who always sorts out group faults without first discussing it.

Hold a backup short account with facts your tutor can confirm, so a missing draft cannot push you to add claims without an audit. A slim account can still count toward your 3. If your format cannot work at all, notify your tutor prior to distribution. Do not put out an additional folio without approval.

A tactful wording could say: "Put your draft in by tomorrow noon so an audit can start. Which part blocks you, and could a buddy aid that part? If it is still not in, our group will opt for that short backup account." This shows a cutoff, a path to aid, and what will follow.

Prior to a tutor audit, hold a draft constant and put all doubts in a joint log. Your tutor should look at your full journal, facts still in doubt, and quotations calling for an audit. Do not tuck doubts into a pupil's own book and put only a smooth draft forward.

Following an audit, a pupil puts faults right and a buddy audits that all tutor points got action. Show that copy to your tutor if your joint plan calls for it. Log which actual draft got approval. An OK for a prior draft cannot stand as approval of additions nobody saw.

Put out only a final copy with tutor approval, following your actual school plan. Hold a final original and a distribution log. This allows a pupil to point to an actual monthly copy if a doubt crops up. It also stops an old draft from acting as a final copy.

Say your box for what's on has 4 May, but a tutor confirms 5 May. Notify your tutor promptly, confirm that fact, and draft a short fix saying which monthly journal and which activity had a fault. Follow a joint plan to contact all pupils who saw it. Modify your original copy with an obvious fix.

Do not act as if your first copy was not put out. Say what was wrong and supply a valid day without blaming a pupil who put it in. Log how it got in: a day your tutor confirms might shift during layout. Add a final day-and-hour audit in your following monthly plan. Do not claim your journal cannot contain a fault.

A pupil might want to put in work anonymously. Ask out of public sight what suits, and obtain your tutor's OK. Hold a log of who did what, out of public sight, so a factual doubt can go back to its author. Public artist tags and task accountability do distinct jobs.

An artist can also opt for an alias or no public artist tag, with tutor approval. Do not ask that artist to justify a privacy option to all pupils. Do not turn anonymity into a drama in your journal. It is simply a joint plan for putting in work.

Following distribution, hold a short talk about what pupils found good, which task ran past its cutoff, and what should shift. Ask for a narrow account, not only a broad claim that your journal was good. Carry 1 or 2 practical modifications into your following monthly plan, such as fact audits prior to drafting or a plain layout.

Finish with a final journal, fact log, task log, and a short handoff for your following job split. Four pupils can sustain monthly work by tracing facts, sharing jobs, and finishing a draft. A good thought about an additional column can wait until a following month; all 4 pupils can discuss it prior to putting it in.

prompt: Explain weighted averages to a beginner through a fictional pottery studio. On Monday 2 pupils each make 8 pots; on Tuesday 8 pupils each make 3 pots. Work out each day's total, the overall mean per pupil and the incorrect unweighted mean of the two daily means. Then compare Group A with 2 successes in 3 attempts and Group B with 8 successes in 12 attempts, showing why equal rates can have different counts. Include two further fully worked examples, a method for checking denominators, and a careful discussion of when combining groups hides useful information. Use only the supplied fictional assumptions, not real-world performance claims. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of natural, substantive English, with no padding.
response:
An avg puts a total against a count. To find output for a typical pupil visit, add all pots and split that total by all pupil visits. A day's avg on its own lacks a crucial fact: how many pupils that day had. Giving both days matching status would omit that fact.

Call our first day A and its following day B. On A, 2 pupils turn out 8 pots for a pupil, totaling 2 x 8 = 16 pots. On B, 8 pupils turn out 3 pots for a pupil, totaling 8 x 3 = 24 pots. B's output for a pupil is low, but its big class turns out a high total.

Across both days, output is 16 + 24 = 40 pots. Our pupil count is 2 + 8 = 10 for all visits. Thus:

Joint avg = (2 x 8 + 8 x 3)/(2 + 8) = 40/10 = 4 pots for a pupil visit.

This count calls for a small clarification. A pupil on A might also show up on B. Our data do not say. Counting visits allows us to work with what is known: 10 visits turn out 40 pots. Calling that 10 distinct pupils would add an assumption. If all 10 visits fall to distinct pupils, 4 is also output for a distinct pupil across this study. If both pupils on A also show up on B, only 8 distinct pupils turn out 40 pots, or 5 for a distinct pupil. That distinction counts if your actual goal is output across a pupil's full participation.

For now, our goal is output for a pupil visit. A faulty calculation would add both daily avgs and split by 2:

(8 + 3)/2 = 11/2 = 5.5.

This puts matching clout on A and B, though pupil counts do not match. It asks for an avg of two daily avgs, giving a small class as much say as a big class. That is a valid calculation for that distinct task, but it is not our joint output for a pupil visit.

You can spot its fault by imagining all 10 visits in a row: 2 with output 8 and 8 with output 3. A row with 2 high outputs and 8 low outputs cannot justify splitting high and low groups into matching parts of that row.

An additional form puts daily avgs against fractions of all visits. A accounts for 2/10 = 1/5, or 20%. B accounts for 8/10 = 4/5, or 80%. Multiply by such fractions:

8 x (2/10) + 3 x (8/10) = 1.6 + 2.4 = 4.

Both fractions add to 1. All visits thus count, without a visit gaining additional clout just for falling on A. Fractions of 1/2 and 1/2 would fit matching class counts, not our actual 2 and 8.

Ways to audit it

Our joint avg must fall from 3 to 8, including both bounds. All individual outputs fit within that span. A total split among all visits cannot put a typical output past both bounds. Our output, 4, fits. This is only a rough audit: 5.5 fits too, so bounds cannot confirm a calculation on that basis only.

Our output should also sit toward 3, as B has fourfold A's pupil count. Think of a group of 5 visits: 1 at output 8 and 4 at output 3. That group turns out 8 + 12 = 20 pots, or 4 for a visit. Two such groups form our full data. This small grouping confirms our formula without an additional assumption about individual pupils.

Finally, multiply our avg by our visit count: 4 x 10 = 40. It brings back our known total. Multiplying 5.5 x 10 = 55 would claim 15 pots not in our studio's log. Linking avg, count and total is a good audit, going past a hunch about what looks right.

In a distinct fictional class mix, A has 8 visits with output 8, and B has 2 with output 3. Now total output is 8 x 8 + 2 x 3 = 64 + 6 = 70 pots across 10 visits. Joint avg is 70/10 = 7. Both daily avgs still stand at 8 and 3, but changing class counts shifts our joint avg from 4 to 7. Daily avgs without class counts cannot fix a joint avg.

Matching fractions, distinct counts

Now look at fictional Group A, with 2 hits in 3 trials, and Group B, with 8 hits in 12 trials. A's hit fraction is 2/3. B's is 8/12 = 2/3. Both fractions match, though B has fourfold A's hits and fourfold its trials.

Adding hits only would miss that information. B's 8 hits do not show a high hit fraction in comparison with A's 2 hits. Counting trials too shows why both fractions match. Also, a matching fraction cannot imply matching totals: a big group can supply many hits without a high fraction.

If our task calls for pooling all trials, assuming no trial occurs in both groups, add hits and trials in distinct sums:

(2 + 8)/(3 + 12) = 10/15 = 2/3.

A accounts for 3/15 of all trials, and B for 12/15. Both hit fractions stand at 2/3, so putting such fractions against any mix of group counts still forms 2/3. Matching clout for both groups would form 2/3 too, as both input fractions match. That lucky match cannot justify ignoring group counts in additional tasks.

Our fractions quantify past trials. Without information about how trials got into a group, matching fractions cannot show matching skill or conditions. A calculation on known data is distinct from a claim about unknown trials tomorrow.

Trial 1: cards in cartons

In a fictional stockroom, 3 small cartons hold 2 cards in a carton, and 1 big carton holds 10. What is an avg card count for a carton?

Small cartons hold 3 x 2 = 6 cards. Our big carton holds 1 x 10 = 10. All 4 cartons hold 16 cards, so an avg carton holds 16/4 = 4 cards. An audit confirms 4 x 4 = 16.

A faulty calculation is (2 + 10)/2 = 6. That puts both kinds of carton on matching footing, as if small and big cartons had matching counts. But 3/4 of our cartons hold 2 cards, and only 1/4 hold 10. Using such fractions puts (3/4) x 2 + (1/4) x 10 = 1.5 + 2.5 = 4.

No physical carton actually holds 4 cards. An avg can stand for a count that no actual carton holds. It is a total split by a count, not a claim about any particular carton's actual stock. Also, our big carton's physical bulk is not a factor in this calculation. Counting cartons puts 1 big carton against 3 small cartons. A calculation on cards would call for an additional look at what to count.

Trial 2: pooling can mask composition

Now look at two fictional groups, P and Q, doing tasks at low and high difficulty. This is only a toy illustration, with no claims about actual skills.

P: 9 hits in 10 low-difficulty trials, and 1 hit in 10 high-difficulty trials.
Q: 80 hits in 100 low-difficulty trials, and 0 hits in 1 high-difficulty trial.

At low difficulty, P has 9/10 = 90%, topping Q's 80/100 = 80%. At high difficulty, P has 1/10 = 10%, topping Q's 0/1 = 0%. But pooling all trials puts:

P: (9 + 1)/(10 + 10) = 10/20 = 50%.
Q: (80 + 0)/(100 + 1) = 80/101, about 79.2%.

Q's joint fraction tops P's, though P's fraction tops Q's within both difficulty groups. This is a shift in composition. Almost all Q trials fall at low difficulty; half of P trials fall at high difficulty. Pooling puts all trials into a joint fraction. It cannot on its own justify a comparison claiming matching conditions.

No claim about which group would win tomorrow follows just from this illustration. This illustration is wholly fictional, and how trials got into a group is unknown. Our task is to spot what pooling can mask: group composition can shift a ranking without a faulty calculation. A valid total can still support a faulty story about it.

For a practical audit, log a group's total output, its count, and what a unit in a count stands for. Confirm that no unit falls into two groups. If a unit can fall in both groups, adding all counts blindly would count a unit again. If groups count distinct kinds of things, stop and find a common basis prior to pooling.

Finally, ask if a joint avg actually fits your goal. It can aid planning total stock or output, but it cannot show all group variation. Hold on to group counts and fractions too. Say which assumptions support a comparison, and distinguish a calculation on known outputs from a claim about skill. Choosing what to count is part of doing this math, not just small trivia.

prompt: Write a complete original story as six journal entries by a small maintenance robot whose stored map gradually fails. Establish its limited abilities and the place it works in early. Its faulty account should become visible to the reader through consistent clues. In the climax, it must choose between preserving its last map copy and helping a stranded person, using only abilities already established. End with a meaningful consequence rather than a miraculous full repair. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive prose.
response:
Log 1

I am Pip, a small robot at a hilltop radio station. My job is small: carry tools, audit doors, and put a lamp in a spot that calls for light. I roll; I cannot climb stairs. My arm can grip a small tool, push a light door, or draw a mark with charcoal. It cannot lift a human. I say this as I favor plain limits. Plain limits form a sound robot.

Our station has a main hall, a pump room by its drain, and a loft atop a long ramp. A rough cord runs along our ramp rail. 3 brass bolts mark its top. A gong cord hangs by our loft door; it is smooth and has a loop. Both cords look distinct. I know that without looking at my map.

My main pack runs my body. A tiny backup pack holds my old map. A switch can shift that backup supply from map to lamp. If I do that for long, my map will vanish. It is my only copy. Our station staff lost all original drawings long ago. I will not draw an additional map as I know this station fully.

My logs go onto a roll at my dock. A map is for work; a log shows how our work fits. I favor that distinction.

Today Ruth asks for a small awl in our loft. I follow our ramp, count its 3 bolts, and put it on a rack by our gong. Ruth thanks Pip. I say thanks is not vital. But I log that Ruth said thanks.

Log 2

I bring our awl back to our pump room. My map calls that room Loft B. I stop at its drain. No rack, no gong, no long look across our hills. I think a tag must now say a distinct word.

Ruth asks why I am waiting by our pump.

"Our loft has slid," I say.

Ruth looks up. "That would call for a big job."

I do not grasp that quip until Ruth points to our drain. It is our familiar drain from my prior log. Our room did not shift. My map has put a wrong tag on it.

I fix a tag and run a short trial. Main hall to loft: ramp, rough cord, 3 bolts. Main hall to pump room: low door, drain, brass tap. Both paths work. I mark this fault in my log, but put our log roll out of sight past a tool box. This is not part of my job.

I call a wrong tag a small fault. But I am also waiting at doors I normally cross without thinking. I turn my lamp on and off, as if lack of light is at fault. Ruth asks if anything is wrong. I say I am auditing doors.

That claim is valid. It is not a full account.

Log 3

My map now holds two ramps. Our station has only 1. I follow its first path and find our pump room again. Its following path stops at a blank patch. I can still spot our actual ramp from our main hall, but my old account cannot match my sight.

I start drawing an additional chart. Halfway through, I stop. Drawing what I spot calls for admitting my old map is faulty. Copying my old map will put its faults in my chart. I put my charcoal down without finishing a path.

Ruth finds my half-drawn chart. "Shall I walk it with you?"

I say no. A robot asking for a companion on a work trip sounds as odd as a clock asking how long until noon.

Ruth says, "A clock can still say it is wrong."

I cannot form a calm word. I ask Ruth to audit our rough cord. Ruth runs a hand along it and confirms that it still runs from main hall to loft. I log that as a finding, without trusting my map.

Ruth puts our awl on my dock. "What is at risk if a map has faults?"

"My job," I say.

"Can you still hold this?"

I grip our awl. Its narrow shaft fits my arm. I can still carry it. Ruth asks if I can put it on a rack, and I do. Both acts follow my usual limits. No act calls for a map of our full station.

"That is only a small task," I say.

"It was always a small task," Ruth says. "You said so in your first log."

I want to say that knowing a station is what turns small tasks into a job. But Ruth has put a gap in my claim. I put our awl down softly. I can still do this much. I do not know if this much can satisfy my wish to work solo.

At my dock I try our backup switch for 1 s. Our lamp glows. My map dims, but shows up as I switch back. I must pick map or light. It was always so; until today this was a backup plan for a crisis that would fall to an additional robot.

Log 4

A storm hits our hill. Ruth walks to our loft to shut its window and bring down our awl. I stay in our main hall with a tool box. My map says Ruth is in our pump room. I know that is wrong. My knowing cannot fix my map.

Our building lights fail. My main pack is almost dry. All day I roll along our paths again and again, to show I still know my tasks. I can still roll a bit, but my lamp calls for a supply I cannot grant from this pack. My backup could light it. My backup also holds my last map.

Ruth calls from our loft. A thin wind-blown board has swung across our landing. Ruth walks around it and cannot find our ramp's top in this black void. A gong sounds, but Ruth cannot find its cord. I ask Ruth to stay still whilst I look.

My map has a door that is not in our station. I almost point Ruth toward it. But I look at my half-drawn charcoal chart and grasp how a bold claim could harm a human.

"I do not know our landing from my map," I say. "I must audit what is actually at hand."

Ruth says, "All right. Say what you find."

No accusation. No call for old Pip to show up first. I roll to our ramp, grip our rough cord, and start up a ramp I can roll along.

Log 5

At our top I count 3 brass bolts. My map calls this our pump room again. I put that claim on hold. Our bolts occupy this spot. Our rough cord is at hand. Ruth calls from past that board.

I can push our board, but I cannot look past it to know if pushing it would hit Ruth. I ask for a location. Ruth taps on our wall to my right: 2 quick taps. I follow that sound with my lamp still dark. My main pack blinks a warning. No long wait can fit into my final supply.

I put my arm on our backup switch. If I hold my map, Ruth must wait without light as my body stops. If I light our landing, my last map will vanish. I thought that map was my only good contribution. It has put Pip in a wrong room on 3 occasions.

I switch.

Light falls across our bolts, our cord, our board, and Ruth's boots. Ruth stands apart from its bottom rim. I push it just far off to allow a path through. This is an ordinary push, within my limits. Ruth walks to our rough cord. I show Ruth our 3 bolts and our way down.

My map falls into blank blocks. I do not watch all blocks vanish. I watch Ruth's hand stay on our cord as Ruth walks down our ramp. I follow slowly, carrying our awl that Ruth had lost.

At our main hall, my body stops by our dock. Ruth plugs Pip in prior to auditing our building lights. My map cannot show up. A supply is at hand; my missing information is not.

Log 6

Morning. Our storm is past, and our board stands against a wall awaiting a fix. Ruth brings my half-drawn chart to our dock. I want an additional map, possibly an instant copy of my lost map.

It is still half-drawn.

"A small part first," Ruth says.

Ruth walks our main hall whilst I roll along. I cannot work solo from an old chart now. I follow what I can actually spot: our drain, our rough cord, our brass bolts. Ruth puts tags in plain sight. I draw a path on a pad, matching all marks to our path. Nobody claims this can fix my faulty map circuits.

My job has a distinct form now. For now I carry tools with Ruth, and ask prior to taking an unfamiliar path. It is slow. On bad days, I am cross at that. I put that in my log too, as a log that holds only triumphs cannot show all our work.

Our pump audit runs past its usual hour that morning. I cannot go to it just as a clock calls for it. I must wait for Ruth, roll along our path, and draw marks that match it. Our dock cannot grant a full path at a look. That loss is actual, and no kind word can undo it. Ruth puts a blank pad at hand. It is an invitation to do slow work, not proof that my old skill is back.

By lunch our chart shows main hall and ramp. Our pump room can wait until tomorrow. I put our chart in plain sight, not past our tool box. Ruth looks at a final row of my log: plain limits form a sound robot.

"Still think that?" Ruth asks.

I think of that blank spot that was my old map.

"Known limits," I say.

I put a tag on our tool box: ASK FIRST. It is a limit I can actually honor.

I ask Ruth which tool is most vital now, and wait for a word prior to rolling.

prompt: Write a complete original realistic story about Boris, an amateur artist asked to paint a small mural inside a village hall. He first assumes the mural should show a grand historic event, but conversations with three residents reveal the value of ordinary daily life. Let those residents contribute distinct concrete memories rather than unanimous advice. Boris makes a draft, receives one useful criticism, and revises a specific detail while keeping his own artistic judgment. Include an ordinary practical setback during painting, solve it using preparation established earlier, and finish with the completed mural and a believable mixed public reaction. Avoid a contest, rival artist, or universal acclaim. Write 2,048 to 2,560 Qwen tokens of substantive prose.
response:
Boris brought a roll of brown card to his first talk at our rural hall. On it was a tall king with a broad crown. A crowd of tiny townsfolk stood at that king's boots. At its top, a flag hung in an imaginary gust.

"A grand start," said Cal, who had put forward this small indoor mural job for Boris. "What is it about?"

"Our hall's founding," Boris said.

"Did a king found it?"

Boris had not actually found that out. His thought ran this way: an old hall must mark an old triumph; an old triumph must boast a grand visitor; a grand visitor must own a crown. On brown card, all this had struck him as convincing.

"I thought I would find out which king," Boris said.

Cal did not laugh. Cal put down a mug and put a hand on a blank bit of wall by a broad doorway. "This is your spot. Think about what fits. Talk to folks who visit our hall."

Boris put his king back in its roll. Cal had said small, and his crown was almost as broad as his full wall. Now this job was shrinking in all wrong ways.

Boris did art for fun. His top work was a painting of a bowl, drawn at his flat, with nobody watching. His worst was a portrait of his dad, which his aunt said had caught his curtains. A hall mural would stay in public. Folks could scorn it without putting it away.

At his flat, Boris built a small trial board. Onto it, Boris put a light ground coat and swaths of brown, pink, and gold. His pad had a drying log. A jar for his brush stood apart from a jar with a RINSING tag. His kit had surplus rags, scraps of card, and a flat brush for broad swaths. His small acts of planning brought comfort following a vast gap in his facts.

On Thursday morning Uma was washing mugs at our hall. Uma had known it from childhood to now. Boris sought an important day for his mural.

"Soup," Uma said.

Boris sat still, waiting.

"Our usual lunch. Long ago, prior to this mug stock, all our cups had grips so small nobody could hold a cup firmly. I would put a bit of cloth round a grip. My husband said it was washing hung up to dry."

"Was a particular lunch outstanding?"

"Most did not vary much. That was why I sought it out. You could count on lunch and company."

Uma took a mug from its drying rack and put both hands round it. Uma's hands had brown spots and a strong thumb. Boris caught that thumb in charcoal in his pad. His plan was a grand occasion. Now a drawing of how to hold a cup was growing in its spot.

"I cannot paint so much soup," Boris said.

"No. You can paint our lunch spot: a broad plank on four stout posts."

Uma got back to washing. Boris did a quick drawing of a chair's curving back against a long board. That arc had a charm his king's crown did not, though Boris was not willing to admit it.

Sal brought back a folding chair that day, following lunch. Boris sought a story Sal would wish to hold onto.

Sal shot a look past him to a cupboard. "My first class."

"What class?"

"Word study. I was forty. I could count sacks at work. I did not know how to turn script into words on my son's school slip. I would walk to this hall on Thursdays."

Boris almost put Sal with a book in his pad, but caught his own hand. "What was in your thoughts as you sat?"

"Our floor. For a half hour. I thought all would know why I was in that spot. Our tutor finally put an inquiry to us: which word was important to us? I said Tom, my son."

Sal was not smiling. Boris put his pad down.

"You can skip my portrait," Sal said. "It was no grand show of skill. I struck out my writing. Our tutor did too. That was a comfort."

Boris put forward a scrap of writing to stand for that class. Sal said it could work, if it was plainly a work in motion. A row of script without a flaw would imply a wrong story.

That night Boris brought his king out of its roll and saw a blank, placid crowd. No thumb, no floor to look at, no son. That crowd had only a task of making its king look tall. Boris put his drawing flat on his floor by his trial board and took up an additional bit of card.

On Friday Linn was at our hall to count chairs for a Saturday ball. Linn took a long walk across it, counting aloud. Boris sought Linn's first account of a ball in that hall.

"It was awful," Linn said. "I took a boy with boots too big for him. My boots had too tight a fit. Both of us sat by a door for half our night."

Boris had thought this account would glow with joy. "Did you marry him?"

"No. I took off for my flat. On my following visit I had no companion and had much fun."

Linn put a hand on our doorway. Folks sat by it to catch a bit of calm in a ball, possibly worn out, possibly waiting for a bold mood. A painting of nothing but whirling pairs would skip all such folks.

"Put in a pair of boots," Linn said. "And room for a soul who has not stood up to join in."

Boris put boots down by a chair in his pad. No portraits of Linn and that boy. His pad had a host of folks now; Boris did not want a full account to shrink into a portrait of who had told it.

His following draft put 3 things around a long board: a mug in two hands, a partly drawn row of script, and a chair with boots down by it. Across from this, a doorway stood ajar against plain light. No king. Boris was fond of that light most of all. It was not drawn from a particular story, but could put all 3 in a spot with room to grow.

Cal brought Uma in to look at this draft prior to painting. Uma took a long, calm look.

"That is a good board," Uma said. "But who can sit at it?"

Boris did not grasp that criticism.

Uma put a hand on his chairs. All stood in a firm ring round that board. Boots sat down by a chair put right up to its rim. No vacant spot for anybody to sit down.

Boris had a sharp wish to say this was art, not a floor plan. Nothing got said until that wish had lost its grip. Finally Boris took out his charcoal.

"If I pull this chair out?"

"That would do much good."

"And shift that script toward this spot?"

Uma was nodding. Uma also sought a big pot in that board's midpoint. Boris did a trial on scrap, but that pot hid his partly drawn script. Boris told Uma why no pot would go in. Uma put both palms up. "It is your painting. I was thinking about lunch."

That did him good. Criticism could modify an option without taking all options away. Boris put a gap round his chair, but his pot did not go in. His light still had its spot. In this final draft, you could join that board without a tight squash among all its symbols.

Boris put Saturday morning into marking his main forms on that wall. His wall's spans and his draft had matching grids. Cal had our door ajar whilst Boris brought his kit in, but took off to a job of his own. Boris did his art solo, with a radio too soft to catch its words.

Boris put his doorway in first. Its light was warm gold, distinct from a blank wall. His long board and its broad arc took form following that. His trial board could confirm how brown would look against gold prior to putting both on his mural. His hands took most of his day. A thumb could look just as fat as a hot dog if Boris did it too fast.

On Sunday his arm caught that brown jar. A thin run of paint slid down his light doorway, right through that gap Boris had fought to hold vacant. Boris stood watching it, clinging to a foolish thought that it might stop of its own accord.

It did not.

Boris sought to scrub that full patch. His trial board lay by his boots. On it, a trial drip had grown broad following a rub whilst paint was still fluid. Boris took a dry rag, caught paint still running down, and did nothing to that blot for now. Boris put a scrap of card atop that jar and put it past his kit, out of his arm's path. First, stop causing an additional fault.

As his patch got dry, Boris put paint on his boots in that mural. Boris had a roll for lunch and took a look at his paint log. Following a trial on his board, Boris put a light ground coat back on that spoilt strip. It took two slow coats and an additional wait. His doorway had lost a bit of its span. Boris took a matching bit off its far rim, so both rims had an inward shift. A narrow doorway now fit his plan.

His light still had its spot in this mural. This mishap had not brought magic charm to his art. His planning had only shown him how to go on without causing additional harm.

By lunch on Monday, this mural was dry. Sal was first to stand by that partly drawn script. Boris had put only a handful of marks in, nothing anybody could truly say aloud. A faint crossing-out was still plain down by its last mark.

"That looks about right," Sal said. "Not so tidy I would think you won a diploma."

Linn was fond of his boots but said his boots struck Linn as too bulky for waltzing. Boris said his boots had not got up to waltz. Linn burst out laughing. Uma saw his chair drawn out, and said nothing until Uma had put an actual chair in front of it for lunch.

Cal brought a small sign saying BORIS. A man by our door sought to know why no king was in sight. That man was fond of royal art. An additional visitor said his hands had too much bulk. A child said his boots should look muddy.

Boris could put forward an account for all such complaints. Only his king got an account: his king was his own fiction, without a supporting fact. Boris was doubtful about his hands. Both might look too big. Boris could look again in a month.

At lunch Boris sat at our actual board, with mugs that did not match and soup that was a bit thin. Nobody put a full lunch hour into discussing his mural. Sal put an inquiry to Linn about Saturday. Uma found an additional spoon. Cal had our door ajar for a visitor with a bag.

Boris cast a look from his mural's doorway to our actual door. His art had room for anybody to walk in. Our hall was using that room without calling on him for an account of it. Boris had his soup, did his mug's washing-up, and put his old king drawing in a box of drafts, intact. It could show him how much a man might wrongly think prior to putting a small inquiry to anybody.
